entry.title: DataFusion: The Rust and Arrow Query Engine Powering Embeddable Analytics

link.title: DataFusion: The Rust and Arrow Query Engine Powering Embeddable Analytics

entry.content:
Modern AI and ML work is, more often than we admit, query-shaped. Before a model sees a tensor, somebody filters events, joins features, aggregates sessions, and dedupes rows out of a lake of Parquet files. Enter Apache DataFusion: an extensible query engine written in Rust that uses Apache Arrow as its in-memory format. It is not a database you install but a library you link into your own application.

For AI data infrastructure, that design pays off three ways. Feature preparation is Parquet-centric, and DataFusion treats Parquet, CSV, JSON, and Avro as first-class inputs. A DataFrame API means analytics code can feed model training without a detour through a separate warehouse. And because the engine is embeddable, your data app and your query engine are one process - no socket hop, no serialization boundary. Subprojects extend the reach: DataFusion Python adds a Python interface for SQL and DataFrame queries, Comet accelerates Apache Spark, and Ballista scales execution across a cluster.

This post is a source tour, not a marketing page: everything below was read from the repository’s main branch, and both diagrams were compiled from the real file tree. Figure 1 shows a query’s path; Figure 2 digs into sessions, rules, streams, and spills.

Figure 1 - A query's end-to-end flow, from SQL text or DataFrame calls to Parquet scans emitting Arrow batches.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • You start at SessionContext, L281, the front door owning shared session state; its sql() method, L612 takes SQL text, while the DataFrame, L220 wraps the same machinery for programmatic use.
  • SQL text first hits DFParser, L439, extending standard SQL with DataFusion DDL such as CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE; the entry point is parse_sql, L593.
  • The AST is lowered by SqlToRel, L442, which resolves tables against a ContextProvider; the dispatcher is statement_to_plan, L221.
  • The result is a LogicalPlan, L267 - an immutable relational-algebra tree. The DataFrame API builds identical trees via LogicalPlanBuilder, L208, and every predicate is a typed Expr, L314.
  • Optimization runs inside SessionState::optimize, L781: analyzer first, then logical rules. SessionState, L133 is deliberately scoped to a single query.
  • The optimized plan is compiled by DefaultPhysicalPlanner, L165 into a tree of ExecutionPlan, L89 operators; execute(), L683 returns one Arrow RecordBatch stream per partition.
  • On the data side, ParquetSource, L282 performs scans with row-group pruning and predicate pushdown, and ListingTableFactory, L30 turns object-store paths into partitioned tables.

Figure 2 - The internals: sessions, SQL planning, rule-based rewrites, streaming executors, and the spill machinery.

Why Rust and Arrow Matter for ML Data

The columnar memory model is the quiet hero. Arrow’s RecordBatch is the engine’s currency: scans produce it, executors consume and emit it, nothing in between re-encodes it. If you train on numeric feature tables, that is exactly your layout - columns of primitives ready for vectorized math. We covered the format in our Arrow tour; DataFusion is arguably its most complete pure consumer.

Streaming matters too. execute() returns an async stream per partition, and spawn_buffered, L173 pushes those streams onto tokio tasks with bounded buffers, so a slow consumer cannot force unbounded buffering. Scanning billions of rows to emit one small aggregate keeps memory tracking the working set, not the table size.

From Install to Your First Model

The quickest poke is the CLI, a small utility that runs SQL on the engine. The official guide gives two commands: cargo install datafusion-cli, or on macOS brew install datafusion. In the shell, CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE points at a Parquet directory and aggregation starts in seconds.

For a real application, take the crate route, verbatim from the project’s example-usage guide:

datafusion = "55.1.0"
tokio = { version = "1.0", features = ["rt-multi-thread"] }

A first SQL query over CSV, from the same docs:

let ctx = SessionContext::new();
ctx.register_csv("example", "tests/data/example.csv", CsvReadOptions::new()).await?;
let df = ctx.sql("SELECT a, MIN(b) FROM example WHERE a <= b GROUP BY a LIMIT 100").await?;
df.show().await?;

The identical job with the DataFrame API:

let df = ctx.read_csv("tests/data/example.csv", CsvReadOptions::new()).await?;
let df = df.filter(col("a").lt_eq(col("b")))?
    .aggregate(vec![col("a")], vec![min(col("b"))])?
    .limit(0, Some(100))?;
df.show().await?;

For a feature-preparation job only the last step changes: call collect(), L1734 and you get Vec<RecordBatch> - Arrow memory ready for a training loader or serialization. Prefer Python? The separate DataFusion Python project offers the same SQL and DataFrame interface. The engine will not train your model; it fetches exactly the rows your model deserves, fast.

Fifty Rules, All in the Open

DataFusion’s performance story is mostly a rule story - and the rules are documented inside the source tree. optimizer_rule_reference.md pins the catalog: 2 analyzer rules, 27 logical rules, and 21 physical rules, in the same order EXPLAIN VERBOSE prints them. The analyzer’s type_coercion rule, L21 inserts implicit casts so every operator receives valid input types. On the logical side, push_down_filter, L45 moves predicates as early as possible, while optimize_projections, L52 prunes columns nobody reads.

Physical planning picks shapes and operators. The join_selection rule, L70 chooses join implementation, build side, and partition mode from statistics, and EnsureRequirements, L74 inserts the repartition and sort nodes each executor requires. A consistency test in optimizer_rule_reference.rs, L41 even fails CI if documented rule order drifts.

Memory, Sort and Spill When Data Outgrows RAM

Embedded engines cannot reserve a warehouse-sized box, so memory discipline is engineered in. SortExec, L1306 states the contract in its header: buffer sorted batches in memory, spill to disk at the limit, merge all runs once input is exhausted. Writing is centralized in SpillManager, L27, which encodes batches as Arrow IPC files and, on replay, wraps the decoded stream in a buffered tokio task.

Aggregation takes the same route: AggregateExec, L863 runs in partial and final modes, and its spill module lets intermediate group tables hit disk. There’s even a streaming join - SymmetricHashJoinExec, L163 - which emits matches as both inputs arrive instead of waiting for a full build side. And for bounded asks like “top 100 per group”, TopK, L100 keeps a small priority queue instead of sorting the world. This is what lets a laptop-sized process crunch a disk-sized table.

Next to DuckDB, Polars and Dask

DuckDB is the closest philosophical neighbor - another in-process analytical engine - but C++ with a server-style SQL shell; DataFusion is Rust, streaming-native, and customizable at almost every point: data sources, query languages, functions, operators. Polars is a DataFrame library first; DataFusion is a planner and executor that also exposes a DataFrame API and full SQL. Versus Dask, which scales pandas across a cluster, DataFusion is single-node alone - clustering is Ballista, Spark acceleration is Comet.

Honest Limits

  • It is a library, not a service: no query endpoint; you embed the engine and build the serving layer, or adopt Ballista for distribution. Freedom, with an invoice attached.
  • datafusion-cli is explicitly a small utility, not a production shell, and has no official Docker image - the docs say to build one from source.
  • Format coverage is broad but not absolute: CSV, Parquet, JSON ship by default; Avro sits behind an optional feature flag in Cargo.toml.
  • The repo README prints no curated benchmark tables; benchmark questions point at external results, so measure on your own data.
  • APIs move: deprecation guidelines exist, and the docs pin datafusion = "55.1.0", so expect version bumps rather than forever-copyable snippets.

None of these limits are hidden: the architecture docs, rule reference, and test suite are unusually candid about the seams - exactly what you want from the layer your features flow through before they reach a model.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Apache DataFusion: SQL and DataFrame APIs, rule-based optimization, streaming Arrow execution, Parquet pushdown, and disk-backed spills - with two architecture diagrams built from the main branch.

entry.title: Apache Flink Under the Hood: A Source Tour of True Streaming, Event Time, and Exactly-Once State

link.title: Apache Flink Under the Hood: A Source Tour of True Streaming, Event Time, and Exactly-Once State

entry.content:
Most machine-learning systems treat streaming data as plumbing: events arrive in Kafka, a nightly batch job in Spark rebuilds aggregates, and the model serving tier reads whatever is freshest in Redis. Apache Flink attacks that gap differently. It is a streaming-first compute engine — its own README describes “a runtime that supports very high throughput and low event latency at the same time,” event-time and out-of-order processing “based on the Dataflow Model,” and “fault-tolerance with exactly-once processing guarantees.” Those are not marketing lines; each one maps to a specific subsystem you can read in the source.

That matters for AI infrastructure more than it first appears. Real-time feature computation is a stateful aggregation problem: per-user click counts over the last five minutes, rolling averages per device, session summaries keyed by entity — computed continuously, not rebuilt nightly, so the model at serving time sees features that are seconds old rather than hours old. Anomaly detection on telemetry is the same shape: windowed statistics compared against thresholds, where late and out-of-order events must still land in the right bucket. Continuous-learning data flows benefit too, because a consistent, replayable event flow with exactly-once state means a failed aggregation does not silently double-count training inputs. Flink’s windows, watermarks, and keyed state exist precisely for these jobs.

This post is a source tour, not a tutorial: we read the current master branch of apache/flink and map the path a record takes from your API calls to a running subtask, and the path a checkpoint takes from the coordinator to durable storage. Two diagrams anchor the walk — a system overview first, then a deeper internals map. One note before we start: Flink’s master has recently been reorganized, and the classic streaming API now lives inside flink-runtime rather than the older flink-streaming-java module. Every path and line number below was verified against the actual tree.

Overview: user code compiles to a StreamGraph, then a JobGraph; the JobManager schedules it onto TaskManager slots, where operator chains run and checkpoint barriers synchronize with the state backends.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • You start at the environment. StreamExecutionEnvironment.getExecutionEnvironment, L2178 hands back the local or cluster environment, and sources are attached with fromSource or socketTextStream.
  • Transformations are just calls on DataStream. DataStream, L111 exposes map, L422, flatMap, and keyBy, L274 — nothing runs yet; each call records a node in the logical operator graph.
  • The plan becomes executable in two hops. StreamGraph.getJobGraph, L1181 turns the logical graph into a JobGraph, L70 of deployable tasks.
  • The JobMaster owns your job. JobMaster, L155 is the RPC endpoint that builds the ExecutionGraph, L81 — now an interface — and drives it to completion.
  • Workers are TaskExecutors. TaskExecutor, L206 is the TaskManager-side RPC endpoint that offers slots and spawns subtasks on request.
  • Subtasks run fused operators. Each deployed task is a StreamTask, L216 executing an OperatorChain, L111, so records cross chained operators as method calls, not network hops.
  • Fault tolerance is a separate subsystem. The CheckpointCoordinator, L103 calls triggerCheckpoint, L575 periodically and CheckpointBarrier, L45 events flow with the data to align every operator.
  • State lands in a backend. For large keyed state, EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend, L98 keeps working set on disk; heap-sized state uses the HashMap backend.

Internals: job submission through the Dispatcher and REST endpoint, slot negotiation, ExecutionGraph scheduling, the network shuffle between ResultPartition and SingleInputGate, and the checkpoint and state layers.

The Life of a Job, From Submission to Slots

Submission is client-side code becoming cluster state. The Dispatcher, L170 accepts the JobGraph and spawns one JobMaster per job, while the WebMonitorEndpoint, L229 serves the REST API and dashboard you see in a Flink session cluster. The JobMaster then negotiates resources through DefaultDeclarativeSlotPool, L88, which tracks the slots each TaskExecutor has offered and matches them to the job’s declared demands.

Scheduling is where the logical graph becomes parallel. DefaultScheduler, L85 walks the ExecutionGraph’s ExecutionVertex, L60 instances — one per parallel subtask — and deploys them into assigned slots. On the worker side, TaskManagerRunner, L110 bootstraps the process. Data movement between subtasks is explicit: a task writes into a ResultPartition, L78, and the downstream SingleInputGate, L128 pulls buffers from it. Because a slow consumer stops pulling, back-pressure propagates upstream as full buffers rather than as dropped or queued records — the README’s “natural back-pressure” claim is literally this design.

Chaining deserves a second look because it is the main throughput lever in that design. The graph compiler fuses consecutive operators into a single task whenever parallelism and partitioning allow, and the OperatorChain wraps the fused operators so each record crosses an internal boundary as a plain method call. That removes serialization, thread hand-offs, and network round trips from the hot path — which is why a word-count job with a source, a flatMap, and an aggregate often runs as one chained task, while a keyBy boundary that genuinely requires a network shuffle is exactly where the chain gets cut and a ResultPartition appears.

Checkpointing: How Exactly-Once Survives Failure

The exactly-once guarantee is not magic; it is a two-party protocol between the job master and every subtask. The CheckpointCoordinator initiates a snapshot and special barrier events are injected into each input stream. When a StreamTask, L216 receives barriers on all inputs, it snapshots its operator state and acknowledges — the asynchronous path lives at triggerCheckpointAsync, L1538. The kind of snapshot travels with the trigger: CheckpointOptions, L40 tells each task whether it is taking a regular periodic snapshot or a different flavor, which is how one coordinator serves both routine persistence and savepoint-style requests. Because a barrier is just a RuntimeEvent, L45 traveling with the records, alignment semantics stay consistent even under back-pressure: the checkpoint divides the event flow into “before” and “after,” so state never mixes pre- and post-failure data. If a task fails, the coordinator discards the incomplete snapshot and the job restarts from the last completed one.

For feature-computation workloads this is the property that matters: an aggregation restart does not double-count the events that arrived during the failure. The barrier alignment is also what makes unaligned and incremental checkpointing possible without breaking the guarantee, though the master branch code behind those modes continues to evolve — treat anything beyond the basic aligned path as subject to change.

Event Time, Watermarks, and the State Layer

Event-time correctness rests on Watermark, L46 — a Serializable marker asserting that no earlier events should follow — and on window assigners like TumblingProcessingTimeWindows, L46 that bucket elements into fixed spans. When you need more control than map or flatMap, ProcessFunction, L52 gives you timers and direct state access. Watermarks ride the same buffers as records: sources emit them, each downstream task observes them to fire timers and close windows, and that is what keeps a five-minute feature window correct even when the input source delivers events late or out of order.

That state is typed and scoped. ValueState, L40 is the user-facing handle for one value per key, held inside a KeyedStateBackend, L36. Which backend you pick decides your memory story: the StateBackend, L81 interface has a heap implementation in HashMapStateBackend, L63 — fast, but snapshots serialize everything — and the RocksDB implementation, which spills to disk and supports incremental snapshots. A feature store aggregating millions of keys almost always wants RocksDB; a small session join may be happier on the heap backend.

From Install to Your First Model

The README is refreshingly concrete about requirements. Building from source needs a Unix-like environment (Linux, macOS, Cygwin, or WSL), Git, unzip, Maven 3.9.16, and Java 11, 17, or 21. Then:

git clone https://github.com/apache/flink.git
cd flink
./mvnw clean package -DskipTests -Djdk17 -Pjava17-target

That Java 17 profile is the default; the README documents -Djdk11 -Pjava11-target and -Djdk21 -Pjava21-target for the other JDKs, warns to set JAVA_HOME correctly, and estimates roughly ten minutes for the build, landing in build-target. From there, the README’s streaming example is your first running job: StreamExecutionEnvironment.getExecutionEnvironment(), env.socketTextStream(host, port), a flatMap that splits lines, keyBy, a TumblingProcessingTimeWindows.of(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) window, sum("count"), and env.execute(). It is a word count, but its skeleton is exactly a real-time feature job — swap the tokenizer for per-entity aggregations and the socket source for a connector, and you are computing serving features.

One practical note: most connectors are no longer in this repository. The README lists them as externalized Apache repos — flink-connector-kafka, flink-connector-jdbc, flink-connector-elasticsearch, and a dozen more — so a production dataflow graph usually involves adding those dependencies to your project rather than building them here. The SQL layer lives in the flink-table module tree if you prefer declarative streaming queries over the DataStream API, and per-key incremental views are also the specialty of engines like RisingWave, which make a different trade-off between latency and expressiveness.

Honest Limits

  • Build friction is real. A Unix-like environment is required for building, the pinned Maven 3.9.16 is strict, and the README’s own estimate is about ten minutes before you have written a line of code.
  • The API surface is mid-migration. On master, the classic streaming classes now sit in flink-runtime, the old flink-streaming-java module is largely a husk, and a new DataStream V2 API (flink-datastream-api, with NonKeyedPartitionStream and KeyedPartitionStream) is growing alongside. Code you write today targets a moving tree.
  • Connectors are separate projects. Kafka, JDBC, Elasticsearch, and friends live in their own repositories with their own release cycles — one more version-matrix to manage.
  • Operational weight. Exactly-once state buys you a distributed-systems surface: checkpoint storage to configure, savepoint compatibility to preserve across upgrades, and a cluster (or a Kubernetes operator) to run — far heavier than a single-process analytics engine that fits on one node.
  • No free lunch on latency claims. The README promises throughput and low event latency, but the right numbers depend entirely on your window sizes, state sizes, and backend choice; we deliberately cite no benchmarks here because none appear in the repository.

For an AI stack, the honest summary is this: Flink is the right tool when features or alerts must be stateful, event-time-correct, and continuously consistent with model serving — and it is heavier than you need when a simple consumer writing aggregates into Redis, or a batch reconstruction in Spark, would do. Read the source with the second diagram open; the barrier protocol and the slot economy explain most of what production Flink feels like.
entry.summary: A source-level walk through Apache Flink's master branch: from the DataStream API and StreamGraph to JobMaster, TaskExecutor, operator chains, checkpoint barriers, and state backends.

entry.title: Presto Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Distributed SQL Engine That Queries Your Whole Lakehouse

link.title: Presto Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Distributed SQL Engine That Queries Your Whole Lakehouse

entry.content:
Presto describes itself in one line in its own README: “Presto is a distributed SQL query engine for big data.” That modest sentence hides one of the most influential architectures in data infrastructure. Born at Facebook to let engineers query petabyte Hive warehouses interactively, Presto evolved into a federation engine: one SQL surface in front of Hive, Iceberg, Delta Lake, Kafka, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch and dozens of other systems, each reached through a clean connector interface. Where Spark’s SQL engine is fused to Spark’s compute model, Presto treats query execution and data access as separate concerns, which is exactly why it spread across the industry and inspired siblings like Trino.

If you work on AI or ML systems, Presto matters to you even if you have never typed its name. Training data rarely lives in one place: features sit in lakehouse tables, labels arrive from event streams like Kafka topics, embeddings and model artifacts rest in object stores such as MinIO, and dashboards over experiment results query the same cluster. Presto is the layer that answers “join this parquet lake with that Postgres feature table and give me a training set” without anyone first copying data into yet another store. It is not a model trainer or a GPU runtime; it is the query muscle that turns scattered artifacts into tabular data ready for PyTorch, scikit-learn or a DuckDB laptop session.

This post is a source tour, not a marketing page. We cloned prestodb/presto at commit e0939e3 on the master branch, read the coordinator and worker code paths, and drew two architecture diagrams from what is actually in the repository today. Every code link below points at a real file and line on master.

The end-to-end data path: a SQL statement arrives over HTTP, is parsed, analyzed, planned and fragmented on the coordinator, then executed as stages of tasks on workers, each reading through the connector SPI.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • A client submits SQL through QueuedStatementResource.postStatement, L213, the JAX-RS endpoint behind POST /v1/statement; results later flow back through ExecutingStatementResource, L99.
  • On the coordinator, DispatchManager.createQuery, L234 mints a query ID, enqueues the statement into a resource group and hands it off for dispatch.
  • Semantic resolution happens in Analyzer.analyzeSemantic, L111, which walks the AST, checks types and enforces access control before any data moves.
  • The optimized relational plan is produced by LogicalPlanner.plan, L185 and its rule-based optimizer chain.
  • PlanFragmenter.createSubPlans, L74 then cuts that plan into stage fragments at exchange boundaries — the unit of distributed work.
  • The per-query orchestrator SqlQueryExecution.start, L491 ties it all together and kicks off SqlQueryScheduler.createSqlQueryScheduler, L158.
  • Splits — the per-task chunks of table data — come from SplitManager.getSplits, L73, which delegates into the connector.
  • On workers, ConnectorPageSourceProvider.createPageSource, L32 opens the actual data stream, and ExchangeClient, L71 shuttles serialized pages between stages over HTTP.

Now let us zoom into the internals.

The detailed view: eight subsystems from server bootstrap to connector SPI, with the coordinator-side planning stack on one side and worker-side task execution on the other.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps the requirements tight: Mac OS X or Linux, 64-bit Java 17, Maven 3.6.3+ for building, and Python 2.4+ only for the launcher script. Building the engine from the project root is a single Maven command:

./mvnw clean install -DskipTests

The README warns honestly that the first build downloads all dependencies into your local ~/.m2/repository and takes a considerable amount of time; later builds are faster. Once it finishes, you can run a coordinator straight from IntelliJ with main class com.facebook.presto.server.PrestoServer, the presto-main classpath module, and VM options that point at the sample config: -ea -XX:+UseG1GC -Xmx2G -Dconfig=etc/config.properties -Dlog.levels-file=etc/log.properties. The Hive plugin expects a metastore address such as -Dhive.metastore.uri=thrift://localhost:9083, which you can drop if you have none yet.

Start the CLI from presto-cli/target/presto-cli-*-executable.jar and confirm the cluster sees itself:

SELECT * FROM system.runtime.nodes;

In the sample configuration the Hive connector is mounted as the hive catalog, so SHOW TABLES FROM hive.default; lists whatever the metastore exposes. For the ML use case, this is the moment it clicks: point a Hive, Iceberg or Delta catalog at your lakehouse, CREATE TABLE AS SELECT your engineered features from wherever they live, and the output table is immediately queryable as a training-set source. If you would rather provision the cluster on containers, a Kubernetes deployment pairs well with object storage in the same cluster.

Inside the Coordinator

Bootstrap starts at PrestoServer.run, L122, which assembles a large Guice module graph and then loads catalogs, function namespaces, access control and event listeners before logging SERVER STARTED. The server is deliberately a composition root: almost everything interesting — DiscoveryNodeManager, L88 for cluster membership, CatalogManager, L29 for mounted connectors — arrives as injected services.

Query lifecycle state is centralized in QueryStateMachine.begin, L225, which walks an explicit state machine — QueryState, L25 enumerates QUEUED, PLANNING, STARTING, RUNNING, FINISHING, FINISHED and FAILED — with timed transitions like transitionToRunning, L851. That explicit machine is what makes the web UI and the system.runtime.queries table trustworthy: they read the same source of truth.

Even the path into the engine is layered. Statement text is parsed by SqlParser.createStatement, L100 inside the standalone presto-parser module, an ANTLR-based grammar with no runtime coupling to the rest of the server — which is why other tools can reuse it to parse Presto-dialect SQL. Submission and waiting are explicit too: DispatchManager.waitForDispatched, L362 lets the protocol layer block until the coordinator has actually handed the query to the execution machinery, giving the client a clean QUEUED-to-RUNNING progression instead of a race against internal state.

Protection against runaway queries is not bolted on. SqlQueryManager.createQuery, L304 registers each execution in a tracker, and a scheduled enforcement loop checks memory, CPU time, scan bytes, output size and written-intermediate limits every second. For a shared analytics cluster serving both BI dashboards and ad-hoc feature queries, that guardrail layer is the difference between a useful service and a weekend pager.

How Splits Become Pages

The distributed execution model rests on three vocabulary words: stages, splits and pages. A fragment from the PlanFragmenter becomes a stage; a stage is instantiated as tasks on many nodes; each task processes splits. NodeScheduler.selectDistributionNodes, L406 decides which node gets which split, balancing load against data locality, while the StageScheduler.schedule, L28 interface lets the engine swap in different placement strategies.

Delivery of work happens over HTTP: HttpRemoteTaskFactory.createRemoteTask, L234 packages a plan fragment plus its split assignments and pushes it to the chosen worker. On the worker, LocalExecutionPlanner.plan, L493 compiles the fragment into local drivers of operators, and data itself moves as columnar pages — batches of typed vectors, not row objects. Between stages, ExchangeClient, L71 pulls SerializedPage batches from upstream task output buffers through the PageBufferClient. This page-exchange design is why Presto can stream results instead of materializing intermediate tables on disk.

Worker-side bookkeeping is centralized in SqlTaskManager, L100, which owns every task the node is executing and reports status back to the coordinator. Tasks are also the unit of backpressure: when a downstream exchange buffer fills, upstream tasks slow their production rather than spill unboundedly, which keeps large shuffles — the join fan-out behind a big feature-building query, say — predictable instead of explosive.

The Connector SPI: One Interface, Many Lakes

The reason Presto can front dozens of systems is a deliberately small SPI. ConnectorFactory.create, L32 instantiates one Connector per catalog name; ConnectorMetadata, L77 exposes schemas, tables, statistics and writes; ConnectorSplitManager.getSplits, L30 enumerates the physical chunks; and ConnectorPageSourceProvider.createPageSource, L32 turns a split into a stream of pages. Splits arrive asynchronously via ConnectorSplitSource.getNextBatch, L27, so slow metadata lookups never block the scheduler.

For AI teams this interface is the strategic part of the codebase. A feature store backed by MySQL, a parquet lake under Iceberg, and an event log in Kafka are all “just catalogs” — queryable in one statement with joins across them, no export scripts involved. Every call into a connector carries a ConnectorSession, L31, the SPI handle for user identity, timezone and catalog-specific session properties, so the same statement can behave differently per catalog without special cases in the engine. Memory governance wraps all of it: ClusterMemoryManager, L106 watches cluster-wide usage and assigns queries to bounded pools like MemoryPool, L45, so one exploratory 200 GB join cannot starve the feature-refresh queries that feed nightly training.

Honest Limits

Presto’s own README sets expectations correctly, and so should you. The build is heavyweight: the first ./mvnw clean install pulls the entire dependency tree, and the README notes the test suite takes several minutes even before you reach distributed integration tests. The supported host list is explicit — Mac OS X or Linux — so a native Windows dev box means WSL or containers. The sample configuration leans on a Hive metastore; without one you will be hand-editing catalog properties to get a first query through.

Architecturally, the same federation strength carries a cost. Every connector has its own capabilities: predicate pushdown, statistics and transactional writes vary widely across catalogs, so plans that look identical on two systems can perform very differently. Presto is a query engine, not a training platform — it will not gradient-descent anything, and it is the wrong tool for millisecond lookup serving, which is what caches like Redis are for. For strict wire compatibility with the Trino dialect you will encounter ecosystem differences, as the community fork shows. And for raw compute-heavy scans, the README points to Presto native, a C++ worker rewrite built on Meta’s Velox engine — a separate execution story living in the same repository. None of these limits are hidden; they are just real.
entry.summary: A guided tour through the prestodb/presto source tree: how a SQL statement becomes stages, splits and pages, and why Presto is the federation layer for AI and ML data.

entry.title: Inside Apache Spark: How One Line of SQL Becomes a Cluster Job

link.title: Inside Apache Spark: How One Line of SQL Becomes a Cluster Job

entry.content:
The best description of this project is the one its authors wrote: the README's first line calls Apache Spark "a unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing." That phrasing undersells what the repository actually holds. Behind that sentence sits a SQL parser, a rule-based and cost-aware query optimizer, a whole-stage code generator, a distributed DAG scheduler, a shuffle machinery, a unified memory manager, and a micro-batch streaming engine — all in Scala, all on the JVM. On top of the core, the same README lists Spark SQL for SQL and DataFrames, a pandas API on Spark for pandas workloads, MLlib for machine learning, GraphX for graph processing, and Structured Streaming for stream processing. One process model, one scheduler, one memory manager, stretched from a laptop to thousands of nodes.

For anyone building AI systems, Spark is the tool you reach for the moment a dataset stops fitting on the machine that runs your notebook. Feature engineering over billions of rows, tokenizing a raw crawl before a training run, deduplicating text before it lands in a vector store, joining click logs with labels to assemble shuffled training batches — these are exactly the "too big for a single process" jobs that single-node engines like Polars and Python-native ones like Dask attack from other directions. Spark attacks the same problem from the JVM side: the engine keeps planning on a driver process, ships serialized tasks to executors, and treats everything — batch SQL, ML training data prep, streaming windows — as DAGs of stages.

The repository rewards reading it. The path from one line of SQL to tasks running on worker nodes crosses a handful of clearly named subsystems, and every one of them is greppable in the tree. The two diagrams in this post were generated directly from the master branch of apache/spark, and every link in the walkthrough below points at a real file and line number you can open on GitHub.

The overview path: the DataFrame and SQL API builds logical plans, Catalyst analyzes and optimizes them, physical planning produces a code-generated plan, and the DAGScheduler turns lineage into stages and tasks that run on executors — with the micro-batch streaming engine feeding the same core.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • SparkSession, L63 is the entry point every session starts from; its def sql, L538 turns SQL text into a DataFrame.
  • Dataset, L125 carries an unresolved logical plan; each select, L1195 or filter just wraps it in another node.
  • QueryExecution, L67 is the state machine of one query: analyzed, L238, optimizedPlan, L361, and finally executedPlan, L404.
  • Analyzer batches, L674 resolve names, functions, and types against the catalog.
  • Optimizer batches, L564 rewrite the resolved plan at fixed point until nothing changes.
  • AdaptiveSparkPlanExec, L71 re-plans the physical plan between shuffle stages using runtime statistics.
  • SparkContext.runJob, L2858 is where a finished plan becomes a job on the cluster.
  • DAGScheduler.runJob, L1886 splits RDD lineage into stages and submitMissingTasks, L3215 ships them out.
  • Executor.launchTask, L551 deserializes each task on a worker and runs it against its partition.

The internals view: Catalyst rule batches, physical strategies, code generation, stage splitting into result and shuffle-map tasks, executor-side storage and memory, and the DStream graph that JobGenerator ticks once per batch interval.

Inside the Optimizer

Catalyst is the reason you can write sloppy SQL and still get fast jobs. The Analyzer, L404 first walks your unresolved plan with fixed-point Resolution batches, L674, binding table names through the catalog and inferring types along the way. The Optimizer, L51 then applies its rule batches, L564 repeatedly — predicate pushdown, column pruning, constant folding, join reordering — until the plan stops changing, and a Finish Analysis batch, L186 cleans up the rest. Only then does JoinSelection, L200 decide, per join, between broadcast, shuffle-hash, and sort-merge execution; large joins typically land in SortMergeJoinExec, L39.

The JVM payoff is WholeStageCodegenExec, L744: whole chains of operators get fused into a single generated Java function, produced by doCodeGen, L780, so a filter and an aggregation over the same rows become one tight loop with no virtual-call overhead between them. The boundaries where fusion cannot happen are the ShuffleExchangeExec, L190 nodes — and those are precisely where AdaptiveSparkPlanExec, L71 waits to re-plan once it can count the actual shuffle output.

Scheduling, Shuffle, and Memory

Below the SQL layer everything is RDDs. An RDD, L84 is a partitioned lineage with just enough information to recompute any lost partition. An action calls SparkContext.runJob, L2858, which hands the DAG to the scheduler. handleJobSubmitted, L2619 builds the final stage via createResultStage, L988, walking shuffle dependencies backward; each shuffle boundary produces a map stage created by createShuffleMapStage, L737. Two task types do the work: ShuffleMapTask, L54 writes its partition's output for the next stage, and ResultTask, L55 returns the final answer to the driver.

Placement is the resourceOffers, L573 loop in TaskSchedulerImpl, L83, which matches pending tasks to the cores that executors have offered. On the worker side, Executor.launchTask, L551 runs each task on a thread pool thread. Shuffle files and cached partitions both flow through the BlockManager, L183, while UnifiedMemoryManager, L58 splits the heap between execution and storage pools and lets them borrow from each other — which is why caching a big dataset and running an aggregation rarely deadlock each other's memory.

Streaming the Micro-batch Way

The streaming/ module is the classic DStream engine, and it is a masterclass in reusing a batch system. A DStream, L64 is just a sequence of RDDs, one per interval. StreamingContext.start, L581 activates the scheduler, and a timer in JobGenerator.generateJobs, L251 walks the DStream graph every interval; terminal nodes like ForEachDStream.generateJob, L47 produce an ordinary Spark job, which JobScheduler.submitJobSet, L145 hands to the same DAGScheduler the batch engine uses. The result: your stream processing literally becomes tiny batch jobs on a clock, with fault tolerance borrowed from RDD recomputation.

Worth knowing when you read modern docs: the README names Structured Streaming as the stream-processing story, treating the stream as an unbounded table over the SQL engine, while the DStream engine diagrammed above remains in the tree as the older micro-batch machinery. Same clock idea, different API layer — and the diagrams in this post map the machinery that both of them eventually land on.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest path, straight from the README: download a prebuilt package from spark.apache.org (no build needed), then start the Scala shell with ./bin/spark-shell. The README's own smoke test is spark.range(1000 * 1000 * 1000).count(), which should print 1,000,000,000 — that single line exercises session creation, planning, stage scheduling, and execution end to end. Python users get the identical flow with ./bin/pyspark and the same one-liner, and it is the natural first cell before pointing a DataFrame at real training data.

Ready-made examples ship in the repo: ./bin/run-example SparkPi runs the Pi estimator locally, and prefixing MASTER=spark://host:7077 points the same command at a standalone cluster (or yarn). If you want to build from source instead, the README specifies ./build/mvn -DskipTests clean package with Apache Maven, and ./dev/run-tests once built. MLlib ships in the same distribution, so once the shell runs, the "first model" is a matter of assembling a DataFrame and letting the engine distribute the rest — no extra cluster software to install for a first run.

Honest Limits

First, the JVM tax. The engine core is Scala and requires a modern JDK to build and run, and the README's build matrix treats Java 21 as the baseline; a source build also couples you to the Hadoop version your cluster runs, because Spark uses the Hadoop core library to talk to HDFS. Second, language drift: the README marks the R API as deprecated, and the connect-based remote sessions show where the project is heading — the classic JVM-embedded session is no longer the only execution mode, but the mature tooling still assumes it. Third, the driver is a real constraint: planning, stage splitting, and task bookkeeping all live in one driver process, so a pathologically wide query plan is a driver-side problem no amount of executors fixes. Fourth, shuffle is materialized — map tasks write files that downstream tasks fetch through the BlockManager, so an unplanned join explosion shows up as disk and network I/O, which is exactly the class of problem AdaptiveSparkPlanExec exists to mitigate at runtime. Finally, micro-batch means latency floors at the batch interval: sub-second streaming is a Structured Streaming and continuous-processing conversation, not a DStream one. None of these limits is a secret — they are all visible in the README or in the source paths cited above, which is exactly why reading the tree pays off before you commit a workload to it.

How It Fits an AI Stack

In a modern ML platform, Spark is the heavy-duty stage between raw storage and anything that trains or serves. It reads from object stores and warehouses, runs the join-and-aggregate grind of feature engineering, and hands off parquet shards or training tables to whatever consumes them. [Kafka](/kafka/) is its natural streaming front door, with the micro-batch engine above picking up where the broker leaves off. For interactive federation over the same lake, [Trino](/trino/) answers the ad-hoc SQL while Spark does the long-running batch; and if your data comfortably fits one machine, the honest comparison points are [Polars](/polars/) and [Dask](/dask/) before you reach for a cluster. The source tree teaches the shape of every large-scale engine that came after it — plan, optimize, schedule, shuffle — which is why it remains worth an afternoon of reading.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Apache Spark on the JVM: SparkSession, the Catalyst optimizer, DAGScheduler, shuffle internals, unified memory, and the micro-batch streaming engine, with two architecture diagrams.

entry.title: cAdvisor Source Tour: How Google’s Container Advisor Turns cgroups into Metrics

link.title: cAdvisor Source Tour: How Google’s Container Advisor Turns cgroups into Metrics

entry.content:
Every serious GPU cluster conversation eventually hits the same wall: somebody asks what a specific container was actually doing at 3 a.m. — how much CPU it burned, whether it was network-starved during a checkpoint upload, or why memory pressure spiked right before a training job slowed down. cAdvisor (Container Advisor) exists to answer exactly that class of question. It is a running daemon that collects, aggregates, processes, and exports information about running containers, keeping per-container resource isolation parameters, historical resource usage, histograms of complete historical usage, and network statistics, all exported per container and machine-wide.

For AI/ML infrastructure, this matters more than it first appears. Training and inference workloads are noisy neighbors by nature: tokenization preprocessing hammers the disk, gradient all-reduce saturates the network, and inference servers wake up in bursts. Per-container CPU, memory, network, and disk telemetry from cAdvisor is what feeds Kubernetes scheduling decisions, autoscalers, and the cost models that attribute a GPU node’s bill to individual workloads. Notably, the stats model even defines an AcceleratorStats type — make, model, ID, total and allocated accelerator memory, and the fraction of time the accelerator was actively processing — so GPU-shaped telemetry has a first-class place in the data model.

This post is a source tour of google/cadvisor at master. We walk the code from the runtime handlers up through the manager’s housekeeping loop, then out to the HTTP API and the Prometheus endpoint. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the tree; the two diagrams were generated from the same reading.

cAdvisor at a glance: four runtime front-ends funnel through one factory into the manager core, whose per-container housekeeping fills the in-memory cache; the REST API and the Prometheus endpoint both read from that core.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The entry point is main(), L108 in cmd/cadvisor.go: it builds the storage layer, constructs the manager via manager.New, L141, registers all HTTP handlers, and serves on port 8080.
  • Four runtime handlers implement a common interface: Docker (containerHandler, L58), containerd (containerdContainerHandler, L38), CRI-O (crioContainerHandler, L39), and Podman (containerHandler, L42). If your stack leans on containerd directly, our earlier containerd tour pairs well with this one.
  • The factory registry dispatches any cgroup path to the right handler: RegisterContainerHandlerFactory, L240 collects candidates and NewContainerHandler, L258 picks one that can handle the path.
  • The raw watcher (NewRawContainerWatcher, L48) uses inotify over the cgroup hierarchy to notice containers appearing and disappearing, feeding ContainerWatcher, L45 events into the manager.
  • The manager (New, L168 and Start, L333) recovers existing containers, starts the watchers, and launches the global housekeeping loop.
  • Per-container housekeeping lives in containerData.housekeeping, L306: each tick calls updateStats (L440), which pulls stats from the handler and writes them into the in-memory cache (AddStats, L107).
  • Two read paths exit the core: the versioned REST API (RegisterHandlers, L51) and the Prometheus collector (PrometheusCollector, L100), which walks all containers on every scrape.

The detailed view: HTTP wiring on top, runtime handlers and their libcontainer delegation on the left, the manager core and event plumbing in the middle, and the stats, metrics and storage layers on the right.

How the Manager Housekeeping Loop Works

The manager’s Start, L333 is where discovery begins. It calls container.InitializePlugins, L335 so plugin-provided factories register themselves, registers the raw factory, then creates the raw inotify watcher and the root container with createContainer("/", watcher.Raw), L357. Recovery follows via detectSubcontainers, L364, and finally three long-lived loops start: watchForNewContainers for inotify events, globalHousekeeping, L443 as a safety net for missed events, and updateMachineInfo, which refreshes hardware facts by calling machine.Info, L426 every few minutes.

Inside each container’s goroutine, housekeeping, L306 runs a timer loop. The interval is adaptive — the next tick is derived from recent samples read out of the cache (RecentStats, L276) — bounded by the housekeeping_interval flag (default 1 second, L48) and a 60-second maximum. Each housekeepingTick, L344 ends in updateStats, L440: the handler’s GetStats() is called (L441), custom application collectors run through the GenericCollectorManager, L27, and the result lands in the cache with AddStats, L505. Two specialist collectors enrich the same stats object on the way through: a perf collector for CPU performance events (L488) and an Intel resctrl collector for cache and memory bandwidth telemetry (L490) — the kind of data that explains why two containers sharing an L3 cache slow each other down, not just that they did. Housekeeping can also be pulled on demand rather than waited for: OnDemandHousekeeping, L160 lets a reader force a fresh sample before answering a query, which is how short-latency API reads avoid serving stale numbers.

Events ride the same core. Creating a container emits an event via addEvent, L913, and destroying one emits another at L957. The manager’s SetEventSink, L35 fans these out to whichever sink is registered — the HTTP layer installs the event manager from events/handler.go, L79 during API registration (L52-L54), and an OOM watcher (startOOMWatcher, L42) wraps the manager to catch out-of-memory kills. For autoscalers watching for evicted inference pods, this stream is often the fastest signal available.

One Interface, Many Runtimes

The whole runtime layer hangs off the ContainerHandler interface, L41: methods for spec, stats, process lists, cgroup paths, and container labels. The Docker factory (Register, L311) decides what it can handle with CanHandleAndAccept, L173 and additionally boots storage-aware watchers for thin-pool and ZFS backends (L202, L235) so disk usage of overlay layers can be attributed correctly.

The interesting trick is delegation. The Docker handler does not parse cgroups itself; it builds a libcontainer handler (NewHandler, L244) and its GetStats, L344 simply forwards to it. The containerd and CRI-O handlers do the same (L214 and the crioContainerHandler path), while the raw handler for arbitrary cgroups and the systemd factory (L29) cover non-containerized workloads — a neat way to watch a bare-metal training process that runs directly under a slice. The shared engine underneath is the libcontainer Handler, L53, built by NewHandler, L65, whose GetStats, L76 turns cgroup counters and /proc snapshots into info.ContainerStats.

Which metric families get collected at all is governed by the MetricSet, L110 toggle set — the standalone binary enables everything except what you exclude, computed in main() at L124.

Runtime support is not hard-coded into the daemon binary; it is assembled at startup through a plugin hook. RegisterPlugin, L189 lets a package contribute initialization logic, and InitializePlugins, L212 — called by the manager’s Start — runs each one and collects the extra container watchers it returns. That is how the Docker, containerd, CRI-O, and Podman support files register their factories and their own event sources without the core ever importing them directly. The practical consequence for operators: building cAdvisor with different plugin sets changes what it can observe, and a runtime that ships a plugin integrates with the same housekeeping machinery as the built-ins.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest path is the official image, straight from the README’s quick start: run cAdvisor as a privileged container with the five read-only host mounts (/, /var/run, /sys, /var/lib/docker/, /dev/disk/), publish port 8080, and detach:

VERSION=0.55.1  # latest release per github.com/google/cadvisor/releases
sudo docker run \
  --volume=/:/rootfs:ro \
  --volume=/var/run:/var/run:ro \
  --volume=/sys:/sys:ro \
  --volume=/var/lib/docker/:/var/lib/docker:ro \
  --volume=/dev/disk/:/dev/disk:ro \
  --publish=8080:8080 \
  --detach=true \
  --name=cadvisor \
  --privileged \
  --device=/dev/kmsg \
  ghcr.io/google/cadvisor:$VERSION

Seconds later the web UI is live at http://localhost:8080/, which redirects to the containers page rendered by serveContainersPage, L166. Your “first model” here is your first scrape: the /metrics endpoint is mounted by RegisterPrometheusHandler, L99, so pointing any Prometheus instance at :8080/metrics immediately yields per-container CPU, memory, network, filesystem, and process series. The collector implements the standard Prometheus interfaces (Describe/Collect, L2177 and L2192), and on each scrape walks every container via GetRequestedContainersInfo("/", ...), L2261. Our Prometheus setup guide picks up from exactly that point.

The same data is available programmatically: the versioned REST API spans 1.0 through 1.3 plus 2.0/2.1, chained in getAPIVersions, L61, with an official Go client in the client/ directory. For Kubernetes clusters, the README’s recommended deployment is a DaemonSet under deploy/kubernetes/ — one cAdvisor pod per node, which is precisely the shape Kubernetes itself uses internally for node metrics.

Storage, Cache, and the Metrics Contract

The standalone binary keeps recent history in the InMemoryCache, L101 — a bounded ring of recent samples per container with AddStats on the write side (L107) and RecentStats on the read side (L126). Longer retention is delegated outward through the StorageDriver interface, L24 with RegisterStorageDriver, L44 pluggable backends, documented in the repository’s storage docs. Machine-level context comes from machine.Info, L56, exposed as node series by the PrometheusMachineCollector, L65, which pulls the cached machine info through GetMachineInfo (L251).

The stats schema itself is the contract every integration codes against: info.ContainerStats carries CPU (per-core and per-NUMA), memory (working set, RSS, page faults), network interfaces, filesystem and per-disk I/O — plus the AcceleratorStats, L914 array with per-device memory and utilization fields.

Honest Limits

cAdvisor calls itself an advisor, but today it is a collector: the README’s roadmap explicitly lists advising on container interference, auto-tuning performance, and usage prediction as future work, not shipped features. Budget accordingly — it will tell you what happened; deciding what to do about it is your control loop’s job.

Retention is the second honest caveat. The standalone binary wires only the in-memory driver (NewMemoryStorage, L42), so its API serves a short recent window; anything beyond that requires an external time-series backend or the storage plugins documented in docs/storage/README.md. Third, GPU telemetry is asymmetric: the model defines AcceleratorStats, but the master tree contains no NVIDIA collector of its own — those fields are populated by the surrounding runtime integration (Kubelet’s accelerator wiring, for example), so verify what your deployment actually emits before building cost dashboards on it. Finally, discovery latency is real: new containers are usually caught by the 1-second housekeeping tick, but the global safety net runs once a minute by default (L47), and very large nodes pay per-container housekeeping cost — the --max_housekeeping_interval and related runtime options exist precisely to tune this trade-off.
entry.summary: A guided tour of the google/cadvisor codebase: runtime handlers, the manager housekeeping loop, the in-memory cache and the Prometheus endpoint that feeds Kubernetes and AI/ML telemetry.

entry.title: Fluent Bit Under the Hood: The C Engine That Ships Logs From Your GPU Fleet

link.title: Fluent Bit Under the Hood: The C Engine That Ships Logs From Your GPU Fleet

entry.content:
Training and serving large models is now a telemetry problem as much as a compute problem. Every GPU node writes journald and container logs, every inference server emits latency and throughput metrics, every fine-tuning run streams progress lines that someone downstream wants to query, replay, or feed back into evaluation dashboards. Fluent Bit was built for exactly this traffic: a lightweight and high-performance telemetry agent designed to collect, process, and forward logs, metrics, and traces from any source to any destination. It is part of the graduated Fluentd ecosystem and a CNCF graduated project, and its README reports over ten million deployments per day and more than fifteen billion downloads — reach it earned by running comfortably on tiny edge boxes and huge clusters alike.

For AI and ML infrastructure teams the agent is attractive for three concrete reasons. First, footprint: it is written in C with async I/O and coroutine-based concurrency, so it can sit on every node of a GPU cluster without competing with training jobs for meaningful resources. Second, structure: parsing raw serving logs into JSON, folding multiline stack traces, dropping noise before egress — all of that happens at the edge instead of inside your log store, which keeps downstream costs and cardinality under control. Third, routing: a single agent can fan the same records out to several destinations, shipping debug logs to Loki while metrics go to Prometheus and traces flow onward through an OpenTelemetry Collector. It coexists naturally with other shippers like Vector, each doing the part of the ingestion path it is best at.

This post is a source tour of the fluent/fluent-bit repository at master, which per the README tracks development of v5.2.0 while the stable v5.1 series lives on its own branch. We walk the data path from a file being read on disk to bytes leaving on a pooled TLS connection, in the same order as the two architecture diagrams below. Every code link points at a symbol that was verified in the actual tree, so you can open each one and read along.

Figure 1 — Fluent Bit engine overview: configuration loads plugin instances, the engine event loop drives collectors, buffered chunks flow through parsing and filtering, and the tag router hands each chunk to per-output tasks for delivery.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Boot. The CLI entrypoint main, L1606 parses flags and config files, then flb_config_init, L281 builds the service context that holds the event loop, scheduler, storage, and every plugin instance.
  • Inputs. Each source becomes an instance via flb_input_new, L326; flb_input_collectors_start, L2939 launches the fd, timer, and coroutine collectors, with descriptor events dispatched through flb_input_collector_fd, L3295.
  • A concrete collector. The tail input’s in_tail_collect_event, L367 wakes when a watched file grows and reads the new lines.
  • Buffering. Records are appended into tagged chunks by flb_input_chunk_write, L773 on top of the storage layer flb_storage_create, L663 provides, which can be memory-only or filesystem-backed for durability.
  • Parsing. Parsers are registered by flb_parser_create, L1051 with JSON and regex backends, while multiline folding in flb_ml_append_text, L707 reassembles stack traces into single logical records.
  • Filtering. flb_filter_do, L121 runs each chunk through the configured chain — for example keep/drop rules in cb_grep_filter, L286 or record rewriting in cb_lua_filter, L434, both able to address nested fields through record accessors from flb_ra_create, L271.
  • Routing. The tag matcher flb_router_match, L140 compares each chunk’s tag against output match rules, and flb_router_connect, L147 wires inputs to outputs at startup.
  • Delivery. Periodic flushing via flb_engine_flush, L198 and flb_engine_dispatch, L360 creates one task per destination through flb_task_create, L551; failures come back through flb_task_retry_reschedule, L291 armed on the scheduler’s flb_sched_timer_create, L869.
  • Observability. The agent instruments itself: flb_me_create, L215 serves internal counters over HTTP in Prometheus format, so you can monitor the monitor.

Figure 2 — Fluent Bit internals: the ingestion path from collectors to buffered chunks, the parse and filter chain, tag routing into per-output tasks with retry timers, pooled connections, and the embedded metrics exporter.

From Install to Your First Model

The quickest way to see the engine move is the README’s build-from-source quick start. The requirements are modest: CMake 3.0 or newer, Flex and Bison, and YAML plus OpenSSL headers. Then:

cd build
cmake ..
make
bin/fluent-bit -i cpu -o stdout -f 1

That single command exercises the whole left-to-right flow you saw above: the cpu input registers a timer collector, the engine loop wakes it once per second (-f 1 sets the flush interval), and the stdout output prints each record as JSON to your terminal. No config file, no daemons — one binary collecting host CPU metrics end to end.

For real workloads you will use the packaged releases instead: the documentation offers Linux packages for Debian, Ubuntu, and RHEL, Docker images, and Windows binaries. A minimal configuration that follows a training job’s log file looks like this:

[INPUT]
    Name   tail
    Path   /var/log/my-train-job/*.log
    Tag    train.job
    Parser json

[OUTPUT]
    Name   stdout
    Match  *

With that file saved as train.conf, run bin/fluent-bit -c train.conf. Every JSON line the trainer writes becomes a structured record tagged train.job, ready to be filtered, enriched, and routed. Two config concepts carry most of the weight here: the Tag assigned by the input, which is the routing key everything downstream keys on, and the Match pattern on outputs, which selects which tags each destination receives — the same wildcard matcher the router applies internally. From here the natural next step is pointing the output at your real destination — a forwarder, an HTTP endpoint, or one of the seventy-plus built-in outputs the README advertises — and letting the same agent handle GPU node logs, LLM serving logs, and system metrics in one place.

The Ingestion Path in Detail

The detail diagram separates what the overview compresses. On ingestion, the engine is not one big loop but a thin event loop coordinating coroutines: flb_coro_init sets up lightweight stacks so that collectors can block on sockets or files without consuming an OS thread each. Collected bytes land in chunks keyed by tag, and the storage layer decides whether those chunks live in memory or are persisted to disk — the difference between losing buffered lines on a crash and replaying them after restart. Inputs that prefer batching can push through dedicated worker threads and ring buffers, such as the one allocated by flb_ring_buffer_create, L42, which decouples hot-path collection from the main event loop. The multiline engine sits beside the per-record parsers because both consume raw text, but they solve opposite problems: splitting one stream into records versus merging several lines into one record. Master also layers a newer processor subsystem on top of the classic filter chain — initialized in flb_processor_init, L1236 and invoked through flb_processor_run, L1800 — which is what powers the SQL stream processing the README advertises as a key feature.

Routing, Tasks, and Reliable Delivery

Once a chunk is flushed, routing turns fan-out into bookkeeping. flb_engine_dispatch walks the routes for the input that produced the chunk and creates one task per matched output; the task owns the event chunk, tracks state, and records which outputs still owe an acknowledgement. Delivery happens on output worker thread pools, and the network layer keeps pools of reusable connections per upstream — connections are handed back for reuse by flb_upstream_conn_release, L964 rather than torn down — with HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 clients implemented side by side under flb_http_do, L2130 and TLS handled inside the connection lifecycle. When an output fails, the task is not dropped: the retry layer reschedules it with backoff on the shared scheduler, and the engine can adaptively retune flush behavior as memory pressure changes. Master even ships a dead-letter escape hatch: when filesystem storage is enabled with the keep-rejected option, the engine’s DLQ path quarantines undeliverable chunks on disk with their tag and the failing output’s name, so nothing silently evaporates during a bad deploy. This is the part of the design that matters most for AI workloads, where a training cluster can briefly saturate a log store and the shipper must ride out the outage instead of losing telemetry.

Honest Limits

A few things worth knowing before you bet a fleet on it, all checked against the README and the tree. First, the README’s performance language is qualitative — “high performance with low memory footprint” is a design goal, not a published benchmark — so treat any specific numbers you find elsewhere as somebody else’s workload, not yours; measure on your own hardware. Second, master is a development branch tracking v5.2.0; for production you should follow the stable 5.1 series rather than reproducing line numbers from this tour. Third, building from source needs Flex and Bison on top of CMake, and platform quirks on Windows and embedded targets mean the packaged releases are the lower-friction path. Fourth, writing a new plugin in C is a real engineering task — the supported extension surfaces are Lua for filters and Go for outputs, which covers many but not all customization needs. Finally, it is a shipper, not a store: there is no local querying story beyond durable buffering and redelivery, so plan a destination that can answer questions, such as Loki for logs or Prometheus for metrics.

Where It Fits in an AI Stack

In practice Fluent Bit becomes the default first hop of your telemetry topology: cheap enough to install everywhere, smart enough to structure and route data at the edge, and reliable enough to retry through broker and store outages. If you want heavier transformation at the edge, compare it with Vector; if your destination is an OTel-native world, putting it in front of an OpenTelemetry Collector is a common and well-supported pairing; and for the stores it feeds, Loki and Prometheus are the canonical log and metric backends. The source tour above should give you enough of the internal map to reason about tuning flush intervals, storage modes, and retry budgets — which is exactly where a well-run fleet separates collected data from collected noise.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Fluent Bit, the CNCF-graduated lightweight telemetry agent — inputs, parsers, filters, tag routing, task retries, and how it feeds AI and ML observability systems.

entry.title: Logstash Under the Hood: The JRuby + JVM Engine That Turns Raw Logs into Searchable Events

link.title: Logstash Under the Hood: The JRuby + JVM Engine That Turns Raw Logs into Searchable Events

entry.content:
Logstash is Elastic’s server-side data processing engine. It collects events from a multitude of sources at once, parses and transforms them with a small DSL that reads like configuration, and then ships each event to a stash of your choice. For more than a decade it has been the default ingestion front door of the Elastic Stack, and even with modern challengers like Vector and the OpenTelemetry Collector it still moves an enormous share of the world’s operational data. If you have ever searched a production incident in Kibana, chances are an event chain very much like the one in this post produced those documents.

Why should an AI or ML practitioner care? Because the same machinery that feeds search also feeds models. Training corpora are born from messy operational logs; LLM serving telemetry (token latencies, refusal rates, error traces) has to be cleaned and routed before it is useful; and analytics on top of structured events is still the fastest way to answer product questions about model behavior. Logstash sits at exactly that boundary: it turns chaotic machine output into typed, enriched, routable events, optionally buffered through a durable broker such as Kafka before anything downstream commits.

This post is a source-level tour of the elastic/logstash repository at its current default branch, main. We rendered two architecture diagrams straight from the tree: one showing the end-to-end event flow from inputs through the queue to filter workers and outputs, and one drilling into the internals - agent convergence, config compilation, the Java execution engine, queues, the dead letter queue, and the monitoring API. Every symbol and line number below was verified with grep against the actual tree before publication, which matters because this codebase drifts fast.

Logstash at a glance: the Ruby agent compiles configs and supervises chains, while the Java hot path moves batches from inputs through the queue to filter workers and outputs, with a dead letter queue for failures and a metrics API for operators.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • LogStash::Runner, L55 is a Clamp command-line class. Its execute, L266 method validates flags, loads the settings registry, and boots the agent process.
  • LogStash::Agent, L48 is the supervisor. It owns the desired state of every running event chain and converges toward it whenever configs change on disk.
  • Config text is parsed by LogStashCompilerLSCLGrammar, L4, a Treetop grammar, and compile_imperative, L23 turns that parse into executable intermediate representation.
  • Input plugins extend LogStash::Inputs::Base, L24; their register hook starts ingestion and pushes events into the queue.
  • The queue is pluggable: QueueFactoryExt, L54 picks between a memory type declared at L70 and a persisted type at L65.
  • Workers are pure Java: WorkerLoop.run, L76 spins on a do-while loop, calling readBatch(), running the compute iteration, then closeBatch() until shutdown is requested.
  • Filters extend LogStash::Filters::Base, L22; each worker invokes filter(event), L151 per event, or multi_filter(events), L170 when a plugin takes the whole batch.
  • Outputs extend LogStash::Outputs::Base, L22 and receive complete batches through multi_receive(events), L101, which is where batching to Elasticsearch, files, or brokers happens.
  • Failures are not lost: the DeadLetterQueueWriter, L106 records events that could not be processed via writeEntry, L441, tagged with the plugin name, id, and reason.

The internals view: bootstrap and settings feed agent convergence; the LSCL grammar compiles configs; Java worker loops pull batches from memory or persisted queues; plugins, the dead letter queue, and the metrics API hang off the same spine.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest “model” you can fit with Logstash is a running event chain, and the README keeps that path short. If you are running it from source, the prerequisites are explicit: JDK 21 with JAVA_HOME set, plus JRuby 10.0.5.0 (the pinned version in .ruby-version). Then two Gradle tasks bootstrap the Ruby side:

./gradlew installDevelopmentGems
./gradlew installDefaultGems

The first installs development dependencies; the second installs the default plugins and other runtime gems. There is a documented bundler alternative (bundle config set --local path vendor/bundle, bundle install, then rake bootstrap and rake plugin:install-default) if you prefer Gemfile-based workflows.

Once bootstrapped, the canonical smoke test from the README is a one-liner:

bin/logstash -e 'input { stdin { } } output { stdout {} }'

That starts a chain with stdin as input and stdout as output. Type hello world and you get back a timestamped event, exactly as the README shows - your first end-to-end flow in under a minute. From there you would normally install real plugins with bin/logstash-plugin install ..., or, if you are packaging your own build, produce artifacts with ./gradlew assembleTarDistribution or ./gradlew assembleZipDistribution. For production use most people just grab the official binaries from the Elastic downloads page, but the source path above is genuinely usable, and it is the only way to debug the engine internals we are about to discuss.

The Queue: Memory or Persisted

Every event chain passes through a queue, and Logstash gives you two very different implementations behind one setting. The memory queue is a JRuby extension wrapping a Java ArrayBlockingQueue - JrubyWrappedSynchronousQueueExt, L43 extends the common wrapped-queue base and holds a blocking queue field directly. It is fast, allocation-light, and completely volatile: restart the process and unacknowledged events are gone.

The persisted queue is a different animal. Queue.java, L104 implements a page-based disk log: events are appended to pages, reads return batches with a limit and timeout, L639, and durability is tracked by Checkpoint, L28, which records page numbers, sequence numbers, and element counts so recovery knows exactly what was acknowledged. Workers drain it through the acked read client - JrubyAckedReadClientExt, L41 extends QueueReadClientBase and materializes QueueBatch objects for the worker loop.

The trade-off is the classic write-ahead-log one: the persisted queue buys you crash-safe ingestion with at-least-once semantics at the cost of disk I/O and checkpoint overhead on every ack. It protects you from Logstash restarts, not from the host disappearing - that is what an external durable buffer is for, which is why so many serious deployments put a broker in front of the engine and treat the local queue as a shock absorber rather than the system of record.

When Events Fail: The Dead Letter Queue

What happens when an event cannot be processed - a mapping conflict, a malformed date, an output that rejects the record? Logstash’s answer is the dead letter queue. DeadLetterQueueWriter, L106 is a final class implementing Closeable that appends rejected events into timestamped segment files on disk. Each record is written through writeEntry(event, pluginName, pluginId, reason), L441, so every quarantined event carries provenance: which plugin failed it and why.

Writers are not created ad hoc by plugins; they are handed out by DeadLetterQueueFactory.getWriter, L83, a static registry keyed by id that also enforces size limits and flush intervals. The engine even has a dedicated periodic poller (the DeadLetterQueue poller in instrument/periodic_poller/dlq.rb) that samples DLQ storage so the monitoring API can report on it.

Operationally, treat the DLQ as a first-class queue, not a trash can: it fills with exactly the events your transformation logic misunderstood, which makes it the highest-signal dataset you have for debugging config changes. Replay tooling exists, and the segment format is plain record files, so a small script can re-inject corrected events - but the discipline of reviewing it after every schema change is what actually keeps data loss near zero.

Observability for the Observer

A data engine that cannot explain itself is a black box, and Logstash takes its own medicine here. The Collector, L28 aggregates counters and timers into a namespaced snapshot backed by a tree-shaped MetricStore, L26. Worker loops increment consumed and filtered counters directly as they process batches, and periodic pollers extend the picture: a JVM poller samples heap and garbage collection, the PQ poller samples persisted-queue disk usage, and the DLQ poller covers quarantine volume.

All of it is exposed over HTTP. The agent constructs LogStash::WebServer.from_settings, L89 at startup and runs it on a background thread; the Rack app is assembled in webserver.rb at L147, and the NodeStats module, L21 serves the /_node/stats JSON snapshot that most dashboards consume. The API is plain JSON rather than a native scrape format, so shipping those numbers into a TSDB usually means a small bridge - the OpenTelemetry Collector with a filelog/http receiver, Vector with its HTTP source, or a cron job pushing into InfluxDB or VictoriaMetrics all work without touching Logstash itself.

The nice property is symmetry: the same snapshot that your monitoring consumes is what the engine prints when a chain wedges, so the numbers you alert on are the numbers you debug with.

Honest Limits

This tour was verified against the main branch tree, and several things deserve plain talk:

  • The engine is not the product. This repository holds Logstash core; the hundreds of real plugins (grok, http, the Elasticsearch output) live in separate repositories under the logstash-plugins GitHub organization, each published as its own Ruby gem. Clone this repo and you get the engine, its default plugin set via Gradle, and not much else - plugin bugs mean cloning a different repo.
  • The dev stack is heavy and the README says so. You need JDK 21 plus a specific JRuby (10.0.5.0), a Gradle bootstrap before the first bin/rspec run, and the README itself recommends the Drip launcher specifically because “the slow JVM startup problem” hurts during development. It also warns Drip does not work with STDIN-based configs.
  • No performance claims were verified. The README carries no throughput or latency benchmarks, and neither does this post. Sizing a Logstash deployment is an empirical exercise; anyone quoting numbers at you is extrapolating.
  • Single-node durability. The persisted queue protects one process on one host. High availability comes from the deployment pattern (redundant shippers, broker in front, load-balanced outputs), not from the engine itself.
  • The DSL is a language. The LSCL grammar is powerful but has quoting and escaping edge cases, and its errors surface as parse failures at startup rather than as friendly diagnostics at edit time.

None of these are disqualifying - they are the price of a decade-old JVM engine that prioritizes compatibility. Know them, and the architecture above will make sense every time you open logstash.yml.
