entry.title: Grafana Mimir Under the Hood: HA Dedup, Tenant TSDBs and Sharded Block Reads in Go

link.title: Grafana Mimir Under the Hood: HA Dedup, Tenant TSDBs and Sharded Block Reads in Go

entry.content:
Every serious ML platform eventually hits the same wall: metrics. A modern inference fleet — hundreds of replicas across a dozen models, each exporting request latency, GPU utilization, KV-cache pressure, token throughput and queue depth — outgrows a single Prometheus long before it outgrows its GPUs. Prometheus is deliberately a single-node system, and once its head block saturates, you are stuck choosing which services deserve monitoring and which do not. Grafana Mimir is the open source answer to that ceiling: a Go codebase that the README describes as “a scalable long-term storage for Prometheus”, speaking the same remote-write protocol and the same PromQL, but spreading both ingestion and queries across a shared-nothing cluster. Metrics are only one leg of the observability triad — traces and logs complete the picture — but they are the leg every autoscaler and SLO dashboard leans on, which is why the metrics database is usually the first component to demand a distributed rewrite.

The pitch matters for AI infrastructure because fleet load is spiky and lumpy. A model launch can double active series overnight; a batch-evaluation night can triple query load. Mimir’s design absorbs this by scaling each role independently — add ingesters for more write throughput, store-gateways for more read fan-out, compactors for deeper history — all backed by object storage instead of exotic local hardware. The README reports internal testing “up to 1 billion active time series”, and equally important for operators, the whole system can start as a single binary: “Using its monolithic mode, you can get Grafana Mimir up and running with just one binary and no additional dependencies.”

This post is a source tour, not a feature list. We read the actual Go code on the main branch of four load-bearing components — the distributor (write front-end with high-availability dedup), the ingester (per-tenant TSDB), the store-gateway (sharded reads from object storage), and the compactor (block merging and garbage collection). Both diagrams below were generated from the repository tree itself, so every file box maps to a path that exists in the repo.

Figure 1 — the remote-write journey: from the single mimir binary through HA dedup and tenant TSDBs into object storage, then back out through ring-sharded reads and compaction.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts in one binary: main, L82 wires whichever components the comma-separated -target flag selects; monolithic mode runs all of them in one process.
  • The write front-end is Distributor.Push, L2284, a stateless layer that validates each remote-write request per tenant and forwards it onward.
  • Before forwarding, prePushHaDedupeMiddleware, L28 collapses duplicate samples from HA-replicated Prometheus servers so exactly one copy is stored.
  • The ingester accepts writes in PushWithCleanup, L217 and appends samples into a per-tenant TSDB head (userTSDB.Appender, L205) protected by a write-ahead log.
  • Once the head is cut into two-hour blocks, shipper.Sync, L108 uploads finished block directories to the object store.
  • On the read side, StoreGateway.syncStores, L396 keeps each store-gateway responsible for a ring-assigned subset of tenants, and BucketStore.Series, L577 streams series and chunks straight from the bucket.
  • The compactor merges block generations in runCompactionJob, L257, while BlocksCleaner.cleanUser, L452 deletes blocks nothing references anymore.

Figure 2 — the detail view: HA dedup internals, the ingester lifecycle from appender to shipper, store-gateway block syncing with lazy index reads, and the compactor's metadata-driven flow.

The Distributor: One Copy of Every Sample

Run two Prometheus replicas for availability and you immediately have a new problem: both push the same series, so a naive receiver stores every sample twice and averages become lies. Mimir’s distributor solves this with high-availability dedup keyed on two configurable labels. findHALabels, L725 extracts the HA cluster and replica labels from each series; whichever replica is currently elected leader for a cluster is tracked in a shared KV store by checkReplica, L563, and the per-sample verdict comes from checkSample, L746 — accept if this replica leads, reject otherwise. The logic lives behind two interchangeable strategies: the per-sample path in perSampleDedupe.dedupe, L84 and a newer per-request variant in pkg/distributor/ha_dedupe_per_request.go. The middleware wrapper in ha_dedupe.go chooses between them, so the choice is a config decision, not a code fork. After dedup, Distributor.Push, L2284 uses the consistent-hash ring configured by toRingConfig, L64 to ship each request to the ingesters that own the series, with replication happening by ring placement rather than by application logic. One implementation detail worth noticing: the election state does not live in any single distributor. ReplicaDesc implements memberlist.Mergeable (ha_tracker.go, L65), so the leader map can be gossiped between distributors with memberlist or held in a central KV store, and every replica converges on the same answer without adding a coordination round-trip to the push path.

The Ingester: A TSDB Per Tenant

The ingester is where samples become durable-ish: each tenant gets an isolated userTSDB with its own head block, WAL and on-disk blocks, constructed by newIngester, L416. Isolation is the whole point — one runaway tenant cannot push another tenant’s WAL past its budget. Back-pressure is explicit: checkInstanceLimits, L190 rejects pushes once in-flight requests, bytes or per-instance series cross their configured limits. The hot path, pushSamplesToAppender, L516, feeds samples and histograms into the TSDB appender with per-tenant validation, and the write-ahead log makes a crash survivable before anything is uploaded. Compaction is a background service: compactBlocks, L345 cuts the head into two-hour blocks and runs local compaction levels, while shipBlocks, L56 periodically pushes finished blocks toward object storage through the zone-aware shipper. After a block ships, the ingester can drop it from local disk — local storage becomes a cache of recent history, not the archive. Memory discipline extends to teardown as well: an idle tenant’s TSDB is detected by isIdle, L520 and eventually closed, so a platform with thousands of small tenants does not pin thousands of head blocks in memory forever.

Store-Gateway: Sharded Reads from Object Storage

Queries older than the ingesters’ lookback need the bucket, and the store-gateway is the sharded service that serves them. NewStoreGateway, L146 wires a ring, a bucket client and a registry of per-tenant stores; ring ownership decides which gateway handles which tenant, and syncStores, L396 creates or removes those stores as ring membership shifts. Each tenant store is a NewBucketStore, L203, whose syncBlocks, L309 keeps the in-memory block list aligned with the bucket index. The clever part is laziness: blocks are not copied locally in full. When a query arrives, StoreGateway.Series, L408 fans out to BucketStore.Series, L577, which consults ExpandedPostings, L82 — postings are expanded against a cached index header, then only the required chunk ranges are fetched over HTTP range requests. For an inference fleet whose dashboards hammer a few dozen series out of millions, this selectivity is what keeps reads cheap at billion-series scale. The index reader also caches aggressively: expanded postings fetched by fetchCachedExpandedPostings, L171 survive between queries, so repeated dashboard panels mostly hit memory rather than the bucket.

The Compactor: Merging Blocks into History

Left alone, object storage would fill with two-hour crumbs. The compactor turns crumbs into history. NewMultitenantCompactor, L380 builds a ring-sharded service where each compactor owns a set of tenants. Its work starts from metadata, not data: SyncMetas, L111 fetches and deduplicates block metadata, GarbageCollect, L136 marks superseded duplicates for deletion, and jobs are planned per compaction grouping. The heavy lifting is runCompactionJob, L257, which downloads a group of blocks, merges them into one, and re-uploads the result — gated by newBlockHealthValidationGate, L586 so unhealthy blocks are not propagated. Housekeeping lives in BlocksCleaner.cleanUser, L452, which removes blocks marked for deletion and cleans up departed tenants. The bucket index the compactor maintains is also what lets store-gateways stay in sync cheaply, closing the loop between write and read paths.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting a working metrics stack is genuinely short. First, download the release and run monolithic mode: mimir -target=all. The entrypoint main, L82 parses that target list, whose valid values you can enumerate with the -modules flag (help.txt.tmpl, L76); the flag itself is documented as a comma-separated list at help.txt.tmpl, L938. The HTTP listen port comes from -server.http-listen-port (help.txt.tmpl, L884). Second, point Prometheus — or an OpenTelemetry Collector — at the push endpoint: the constant PrometheusPushEndpoint = "/api/v1/push" is defined at api.go, L298 and registered on the distributor handler at api.go, L309. Third, verify data is flowing by querying the Prometheus-compatible API, which is served under the /prometheus URL prefix configured at api.go, L95 — your GPU-utilization panels now survive ingester restarts. For production, split -target values across a cluster and point block storage at S3 or GCS; wiring the deployment with a Kubernetes operator is covered in our /prometheus-operator/ tour, while the tracing counterpart for the same fleet is /tempo/, its log sibling is /loki/, and the alternative bucket-architecture comparison is /thanos/.

Honest Limits

This tour reads four pkg subdirectories plus pkg/api from the main branch; the querier, query-frontend, ruler and alertmanager services are unexamined, and the query path beyond the store-gateway is out of scope. We traced the per-sample HA dedup strategy in depth; the per-request variant exists in the tree but was not followed line by line. The HA-tracker discussion also assumes some KV-store backend holds the leader map — which backend (gossip-based memberlist versus Consul) fits you is a deployment decision this post deliberately leaves open. The “1 billion active time series” figure is Grafana’s own internal-testing claim quoted from the README — we ran no benchmarks of our own and none are implied. The diagrams omit the query-frontend, ruler and alertmanager for legibility. Line numbers refer to the tree as of today; the codebase moves quickly, and recent work on Kafka-backed ingest storage is visible in flags and tests. None of the claims here should be treated as sizing advice without your own load tests.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of Grafana Mimir showing how the distributor, ingester, store-gateway and compactor turn Prometheus remote-write into horizontally scalable metrics storage.

entry.title: Pyroscope: A Source Tour of Grafana’s Continuous Profiling Backend

link.title: Pyroscope: A Source Tour of Grafana’s Continuous Profiling Backend

entry.content:
Anyone who has served a large language model in production knows the feeling: the GPU sits at 97% utilization on your dashboard, yet tokens per second quietly sag during the evening peak. Dashboards built on metrics from Prometheus tell you that something slowed down; they rarely tell you which function is responsible. Continuous profiling closes that gap. Instead of a handful of counters, it records always-on samples of where CPU time and allocations actually go — stack frame by stack frame — for every process in the fleet, at a fraction of the cost of running a debugger.

That capability matters enormously for AI and ML infrastructure. A Python inference server wrapped around a C++ runtime spends time in surprising places: tokenizers, vendored HTTP layers, CUDA driver calls, serialization glue between the scheduler and the model. A training loop that leaks a copy-per-step shows up as a memory flame graph that grows without bound. Even the Go binaries that typically sit in front of your models — gateways, routers, token-bucket rate limiters — have hot paths worth watching. With a profiler like Pyroscope running always-on, these hot spots surface as flame graphs you can diff over time, not as anecdotes you reproduce under a debugger after the incident.

Grafana Pyroscope is the open-source continuous profiling backend in the Grafana observability stack, alongside logging with Loki and tracing with Tempo. Its 2.0 release made a bold architectural call: profiles are written directly to object storage, removing in-memory ingesters and local disks from the default path — simplifying operations and lowering resource usage at scale. We cloned the repository, read the Go source, and traced one profile sample from the HTTP push endpoint all the way to a flame graph. The two diagrams below were generated from the actual code layout.

Pyroscope at a glance: ingestion fans out through a distributor, the v2 write path lands segments in object storage with a raft-backed metastore index, and queries are planned across blocks and merged into flame graphs.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Push endpoint. Every profile arrives at the push API. RegisterDistributor, L276 wires the endpoints, and a capture wrapper can sample incoming profiles for debugging (registerPusher, L17).
  • Distributor.Push, L326 is the workhorse. It parses each raw pprof sample with a hard cap on decompressed size (RawFromBytesWithLimit, L103), rejects batches that exceed per-tenant body limits, and enforces ingestion rate limits before anything is stored.
  • Router.Send, L89 then picks a write path per tenant: the new segment-writer path, the legacy ingester path, or both during migration.
  • Segment writer. On the v2 path, profiles land in ordered write shards (segmentsWriter, L44) that feed in-memory heads (Head.Ingest, L80). Periodically each segment flushes (segment.flush, L221): heads are concatenated into one block file, the block is uploaded, and its metadata is registered.
  • Metastore. Block metadata is committed through a raft-replicated index. IndexService.AddBlock, L71 fronts the handler that applies these commands to replicated state (IndexCommandHandler.AddBlock, L61).
  • Compaction. In the background, NewMultitenantCompactor, L285 plans work per tenant and leases jobs to a dedicated Worker, L84 that merges low-level blocks into bigger, cheaper-to-read ones.
  • Query frontend. On reads, the read-path router (Query, L69) splits ranges by time and hands newer data to the v2 frontend (NewQueryFrontend, L141), which fetches block metadata, builds a balanced plan, and invokes backends.
  • QueryBackend.Invoke, L101 executes the plan’s MERGE and READ nodes; the block reader (NewBlockReader, L73) fetches only the datasets a query needs and merges samples into a response.
  • Legacy path. The v1 querier still fans out to in-memory ingesters and block-serving gateways (Querier.selectSeries, L1124, NewStoreGateway, L87) — the mode many production clusters run today.

The detailed view: ingestion internals, both write paths, storage and compaction machinery, and the two query paths side by side.

From Push to Object Storage: The v2 Write Path

The v2 write path is a study in doing less, on purpose. The distributor deliberately stays thin: parse, validate, route. Parsing is where the first hard engineering constraint appears. Profiles arrive gzipped inside protobuf envelopes, and decompression is a memory-amplification risk when tenants push large batches, so RawFromBytesWithLimit, L103 refuses payloads once the decompressed size crosses a per-tenant limit — the distributor counts discarded bytes and profiles into distinct metrics so you can see the policy biting.

Routing is the second constraint. The write-path router exists because the codebase must serve two storage architectures simultaneously. A tenant on the v2 path gets its series sent to segment writers; a tenant still on v1 gets the classic dskit ring treatment; and the combined path duplicates writes so tenants can migrate without a cutover. This is the same philosophy that lets Mimir and Loki evolve their storage without breaking clients: the write API stays frozen, the machinery behind it changes.

Inside the segment writer, the design revolves around sharding by tenant and service name. Each shard is a single-writer loop — ordered, contention-free — that accumulates samples in an in-memory head keyed by dataset. When the head grows large enough or old enough, the flush sequence in segment.flush, L221 concatenates dataset heads into a single block file, appends the tenant dataset index built by NewDatasetIndexWriter, L53, encodes block metadata, uploads the result through the object-storage bucket abstraction (Bucket, L14), and finally registers the block with the metastore. Only after that commit is the data durable and queryable — everything before is replayable in-memory state.

The bucket abstraction is what makes deployment boring in the good sense. A factory (NewBucket, L21) constructs clients for S3, GCS, Azure, Swift, or a filesystem, so a lab setup and a global fleet differ by configuration, not code. If you already run a MinIO endpoint for model artifacts, the same object store can serve your profile blocks — one more reason this architecture pairs well with an existing /minio/ deployment.

The Metastore and Compaction: Small Files Are the Enemy

Object storage is cheap per byte and expensive per request. A busy cluster writing one small segment per writer-shard per interval would generate a request storm, so compaction is not optional hygiene — it is the mechanism that keeps query-time request counts sane. The metastore records each block with a compaction level; the multitenant compactor plans which groups of blocks can merge, and a separate worker executes the merges, rewrites block files at the next level, and reports the new metadata back through the metastore’s compaction service (NewCompactionService, L29).

Separating planning (a ring-sharded, stateful component) from execution (a stateless worker that leases jobs) is a deliberate scaling choice: compaction throughput can be scaled independently of cluster ownership. The metastore itself is raft-replicated, which is notable — many metadata layers in this ecosystem lean on external stores like etcd or object-storage-backed catalogs, while Pyroscope keeps its block index as a self-contained, strongly consistent service.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest path from nothing to a live flame graph is a single container: docker run -it -p 4040:4040 grafana/pyroscope. On macOS or Linux, brew install pyroscope-io/brew/pyroscope followed by brew services start pyroscope does the same via Homebrew. If you prefer binaries, download the archive from the latest release, tar xvf pyroscope_*.tar.gz, and run ./pyroscope. The server listens on port 4040.

Now feed it profiles. For a Python model server, add the Python SDK and point it at your process — the repository carries runnable examples under examples/language-sdk-instrumentation/python, alongside Go, Java, Ruby, Node.js, .NET, and Rust examples. For fleet-wide coverage without touching code, Grafana Alloy can pull profiles, and OTLP ingestion accepts profiles from OpenTelemetry-compatible sources such as the OpenTelemetry eBPF profiler — handy when your GPU hosts are otherwise instrumented through the /opentelemetry-collector/. Query side, open Grafana Profiles Drilldown: with the OSS stack it is pre-installed, and you can start from a service selector, pick a profile type (CPU, allocs), and scrub the timeline. If you already run Grafana with /loki/ for logs or a tracing backend for spans, profiles complete the picture: logs tell you the error, traces tell you the slow span, and the profile tells you the line of code that burned the CPU inside that span.

A useful habit for AI workloads: record a flame graph of your inference server at a known-good token throughput, then diff it against a slow period. The delta is usually a handful of frames — a fallback tokenizer path, a retry storm in a client library, a Python-level preprocessing loop — and it appears in minutes, not after a reproduction hunt.

The Legacy v1 Path Still Matters

Why does the old architecture still occupy so much of the tree? Because migrations are long and the operators are real. In v1, Ingester.Push, L336 routes to per-tenant instances (newInstance, L32), each wrapping a local PhlareDB database (New, L117) that ingests into an in-memory head (NewHead, L83), flushes parquet-backed blocks, and ships them to shared storage (Shipper, L76). Queries then fan out to ingesters for recent data and to store-gateways for historical blocks, with bidirectional streaming merge clients pooled per ring (NewIngesterPool, L36). Reading both paths is genuinely instructive: the v2 segment writer is essentially the distillation of everything the team learned running PhlareDB at scale.

Honest Limits

Continuous profiling is sampling, so very short, rare execution spikes can slip between samples; the picture is statistical and strongest for steady-state behavior. The 2.0 architecture is new — the README notes existing v1 deployments opt in via a flag and migrate without data loss, which means mixed-fleet operation and its router complexity are your reality for a while. The v2 write path assumes object storage; there is no local-disk default anymore, so even a modest single-node deployment needs a bucket endpoint (the filesystem provider covers the simplest cases). The README’s quick start is a single local container; running the microservice modules in production means operating rings, the metastore’s raft cluster, and compaction workers — real operational surface, documented in the upstream deployment guides rather than bundled into one command. And licensing is AGPLv3, which some organizations need to review before embedding Pyroscope in a commercial offering. None of these are reasons to skip profiling; they are the costs of a backend that treats profiles as first-class, queryable data at fleet scale.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Grafana Pyroscope's v2 architecture: distributors, segment writers, object storage, the metastore, compaction, and the query path that turns pprof samples into flame graphs for AI and ML infrastructure.

entry.title: Inside Apache SkyWalking: A Source Tour of the OAP Server That Watches AI Infrastructure

link.title: Inside Apache SkyWalking: A Source Tour of the OAP Server That Watches AI Infrastructure

entry.content:
Modern AI infrastructure is a distributed-systems problem wearing a lab coat. One “ask the model” request can cross a gateway, a queue, a vector database, and a GPU inference service — and when latency spikes, someone must find which hop burned the milliseconds. Apache SkyWalking, the Apache Software Foundation’s observability platform, exists for exactly that diagnosis: it collects traces, metrics, logs, and events, aggregates them in a backend called the OAP server, and serves results through a UI and a GraphQL API. Most Java-based AI serving stacks — Spring Boot gateways, gRPC front ends, Kafka consumers feeding batch inference — are pure JVM workloads, so a Java-native APM is often the fastest way to see what your AI platform really does at runtime. And because the same platform also ingests OpenTelemetry data, the Python and Go services around the JVM can join the same topology instead of living in a separate monitoring silo.

This post is a source tour of that backend. We read the master branch of apache/skywalking and follow one story through the Java source: telemetry arrives at receivers, is dispatched into Open Assessment Language (OAL) analysis, merges through two levels of in-memory aggregation, persists into pluggable storage, and returns through the GraphQL query layer. One caveat, verified against the repository: since SkyWalking 9 the Java agent lives in the sibling repo apache/skywalking-java; the repo explored here holds the OAP server, protocols, and the analysis engine.

Why does this matter for AI workloads? Because the core has grown first-class concepts for them. server-core contains AIAgentSessionFlowRecord, annotated for the AI_AGENT_SESSION_FLOW scope, and GenAIEvaluationRecord, which stores GenAI evaluation results as queryable data. In other words, the same engine that aggregates service latency also aggregates token usage and evaluation outcomes, so an LLM gateway can be debugged with the same tools as the REST services behind it. Observability platforms are quietly becoming control planes for LLM applications, and these record types are where that convergence shows up in code.

The ten-thousand-meter view: receivers ingest agent and OTLP traffic on the left, the analysis core turns telemetry into Metrics, L1/L2 workers aggregate and persist, and the query module serves GraphQL on the right.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Every gRPC endpoint is published through a shared server: receivers register on the GRPCHandlerRegister, L26 interface.
  • The trace entry point is TraceSegmentReportServiceHandler, L39; its streaming collect (L63) forwards each segment to the parser via send (L73).
  • OpenTelemetryMetricHandler, L38 accepts OTLP export (L74) — so any OpenTelemetry SDK, including ones on Python or Go AI services, can feed SkyWalking.
  • DispatcherManager.forward, L45 routes parsed sources to OAL-generated dispatchers by scope.
  • All metric types extend abstract Metrics, L41, whose combine (L68) is the merge primitive everything builds on.
  • MetricsStreamProcessor.in, L141 is the hot path handing each metric to its per-class L1 worker; create (L165) assembles that chain at registration.
  • The query side composes one executable schema in GraphQLQueryProvider.prepare, L102.

The detailed view: shared gRPC/HTTP registries, trace and OTLP receivers, the OAL dispatch layer, L1 aggregation workers, L2 persistence workers, and the GraphQL stack, with paths verified on master.

A Module System All the Way Down

The backend is a module container, not one big application class. Each capability is a ModuleDefine plus a ModuleProvider resolved at boot; the central CoreModule, L82 declares the name "core" on L83, with storage, query, telemetry, and analyzer modules plugging alongside. A starter module assembles the chosen providers into a runnable server, which is why the same codebase powers both a full application server and lighter deployment modes. That indirection is why storage backends are swappable — providers are looked up by interface, never hard-wired.

Receiver wiring shows the payoff. TraceModuleProvider.start() on L62 fetches the shared GRPCHandlerRegister and adds its handlers; the OTLP provider (L38) does the same. One process exposes many ingestion protocols on shared ports with no per-receiver socket code.

Receivers: Where Telemetry Enters

Receivers are deliberately thin. The streaming trace handler wraps its parse call in a histogram timer and error counter, so ingestion latency is itself a SkyWalking metric — the codebase observes itself, which matters when you are diagnosing the diagnostician during a traffic storm. A REST twin exists for gRPC-blocked environments (TraceSegmentReportHandler, L38), and a compatibility handler keeps older agent protocol versions alive.

The OTLP receiver matters most for AI infrastructure. It delegates to OpenTelemetryMetricRequestProcessor.processMetricsRequest, L149, replaying samples through registered MAL converters — Meter Analysis Language rules that translate arbitrary OTLP gauges into SkyWalking metrics. If you already push metrics from an inference gateway, the same traffic lands here via a rule file instead of new code. The repo also ships Zipkin ingestion modules, which pairs nicely with our Zipkin architecture tour when consolidating an existing trace estate.

OAL and the Two-Level Metrics Aggregation

This is the heart. OAL, the Open Assessment Language, is SkyWalking’s answer to the question every APM eventually faces: how do you turn an unbounded firehose of raw spans into a bounded set of aggregate metrics without hand-writing aggregation code per feature? The answer is a small declarative language whose script files name the metrics, their scopes, and their functions, and a compiler that turns those declarations into ordinary Java classes at build time. At runtime, DispatcherManager.forward, L45 calls the dispatchers registered for a source’s scope — the generated SegmentDispatcher.dispatch, L29 handles raw traces, which end as SegmentRecords, L47, persisted through the record stream.

Metrics take a two-level ride, and the class comments in the source describe the design candidly. L1 is in-memory merging: MetricsAggregateWorker (L57) shares one adaptive queue across metric types, accepts items at in, L146, merges them in a MergableBufferedData.accept, L49 cache keyed by entity and time bucket, and pushes merged buckets onward in flush (L178). In a cluster, MetricsRemoteWorker, L33 ships each bucket to the node owning its hash slot, so aggregation work is distributed across the OAP nodes instead of hammering one of them.

L2 is persistence. MetricsPersistentWorker.in (L172) buffers metrics in a 70-second session cache so repeated writes to one entity collapse into a single database operation, and buildBatchRequests (L188) turns expired sessions into batch writes through IBatchDAO, L30, the interface every storage plugin implements. Down-sampling is explicit: Metrics demands toHour (L80) and toDay (L87) clones, and a transitive worker fans minute data to hour and day workers. Streams register storage models through the ModelRegistry, L33 interface. The same write-amplification-versus-read-speed tension we studied in Grafana Mimir and Tempo reappears here — solved inside the application instead of the database.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting a live topology takes two downloads. First, start the OAP server and UI from the distribution built from this repo’s apm-dist module; the documented defaults are gRPC ingestion on 11800, HTTP on 12800, UI on 8080. Second, attach the agent from apache/skywalking-java to your JVM-based AI service:

java -javaagent:/opt/skywalking-agent/skywalking-agent.jar \
     -Dskywalking.agent.service_name=inference-gateway \
     -Dskywalking.collector.backend_service=oap:11800 \
     -jar inference-gateway.jar

Refresh the UI and the topology appears — nodes for your services, edges for their calls, latency percentiles per endpoint, all derived from the segments your first requests produced. No code changes, no SDK calls. If you prefer containers, the repo’s docker directory and the published images let you run the OAP server and UI as two containers with a shared network, which is convenient when the observability stack should live and die with a Kubernetes namespace rather than a host. For the non-JVM parts of the AI stack — a Python model server, a Go preprocessor — point an OpenTelemetry SDK at the OTLP receiver above; the OpenTelemetry Collector can sit in front as a buffer for retries and multiplexing. Minutes later you have what every ML platform team needs: which endpoint is slow, whether errors cluster on a dependency, and how AI-agent sessions actually flow through the system.

Querying: GraphQL and MQE

Everything the UI renders arrives through one protocol. The QueryModule, L26 defines the "query" module; the GraphQL provider’s prepare() composes the schema file by file — metadata, topology, traces, logs, alarms, profiling, AI-agent conversations — and start() (L176) mounts the executable schema as GraphQLQueryHandler, L41 behind the shared HTTP registry.

Beneath the resolvers sit plain services: TraceQueryService.queryBasicTraces (L119) pages through stored summaries, TopologyQueryService.getGlobalTopology (L92) assembles the service graph, and MetricsQueryService, L44 serves metric series. The twist since 9.5 is MQE, a Metrics Query Expression language evaluated by MQEExecutor, L52 at query time — dashboards can compute ratios like p99-latency-per-request without new storage code. Because the schema is introspectable GraphQL, you can also query it from any client: a notebook, a CI job that fails when error rates cross a threshold, or a custom SRE bot that pulls topology snapshots into your chat tool.

Honest Limits

Everything above is limited to what the source and repository layout support; no benchmarks were run for this article. First, this repo does not contain the Java agent — since the 9.x split, Byte Buddy instrumentation and agent configuration live in apache/skywalking-java, so agent behavior belongs to that project’s source, and any statement about which frameworks it instruments should be checked against its documentation. Second, the numbers quoted (a 20,000-slot L1 buffer, a 500 ms flush period, a 70-second session) are source-level defaults in the cited classes; they are tunable, and real behavior under your traffic is knowable only from your load tests. Third, aggregation relies on OAL code generated at build time — generated dispatcher classes do not exist in the source tree until you build the project, and reading master means reading a moving target, so treat line numbers here as a snapshot of one commit rather than a stable API. Fourth, the AI-agent and GenAI record types are present and queryable, but how well they model real LLM workloads is a question only your data can answer. Finally, the IBatchDAO contract is backend-agnostic by design, so any performance statement about BanyanDB or Elasticsearch must come from those implementations’ own documentation, never from this tour.
